procedures_performed: Cycle six of CIVI-CAD (Cytoxan, Adriamycin, and DTIC) from 07/22/2008 to 07/29/2008.
CTA, chest PE study showing no evidence for pulmonary embolism.
Head CT showing no evidence of acute intracranial abnormalities.
Sinus CT, normal mini-CT of the paranasal sinuses.

Leiomyosarcoma, the patient was admitted to Hem/Onco B Service under attending Dr.
XYZ for cycle six of continuous IV infusion Cytoxan, Adriamycin, and DTIC, which she
tolerated well.

History of pulmonary embolism. Upon admission, the patient reported an approximate
two-week history of dyspnea on exertion and some mild chest pain. She underwent a CTA,

which showed no evidence of pulmonary embolism and the patient was started on
prophylactic doses of Lovenox at 40 mg a day. She had no further complaints throughout the
hospitalization with any shortness of breath or chest pain.

History of subdural hematoma, also on admission the patient noted some mild intermittent
headaches that were fleeting in nature, several a day that would resolve on their own. Her
headaches were not responding to pain medication and so on 07/24/2008, we obtained a
head CT that showed no evidence of acute intracranial abnormalities. The patient also had a
history of sinusitis and so a sinus CT scan was obtained, which was normal.

Pancytopenia. On admission, the patient's white blood count was 3.4, hemoglobin 11.3,
platelet count 82, and ANC of 2400. The patient's counts were followed throughout admission.
She did not require transfusion of red blood cells or platelets; however, on 07/26/2008 her
ANC did dip to 900 and she was placed on neutropenic diet. At discharge her ANC is back up
to 1100 and she is taken off neutropenic diet. Her white blood cell count at discharge was 1.4
and her hemoglobin was 11.2 with a platelet count of 140.

History of pneumonia. During admission, the patient did not exhibit any signs or symptoms
of pneumonia.

diagnosis_explanation:
Leiomyosarcoma is a type of cancer. It starts in muscle tissue. It can grow in many parts of the body.

You have a history of blood clots in your lungs. This is called a pulmonary embolism. You also had bleeding in your brain. This is called a subdural hematoma. You have a low number of blood cells. This is called pancytopenia. You also had an infection in your lungs. This is called pneumonia.
medication_rationale:
Lovenox 40 mg:
This medicine is a blood thinner. It helps stop blood clots from forming. This can be important when you have cancer. You might notice some bruising. This is common and usually not a problem. Call your doctor if you see any blood in your urine or stool.

Important: Do not stop taking this medicine without calling your doctor first.
recovery_trajectory:
**Week 1:**
- You may feel tired after your treatment.
- You might have some mild nausea or a headache.
- Rest when you feel you need to.
- You can eat your regular diet.
- Watch for fevers higher than 100.5 degrees Fahrenheit.
- Your goal this week is to rest and recover at home.
- Call your doctor if you have a fever over 100.5.

**Week 2:**
- You may start to feel a little more energy this week.
- Continue to rest when you are tired.
- Eat your regular diet.
- Your headache should continue to get better.
- Watch for fevers over 100.5 degrees Fahrenheit.
- Your goal this week is to do short walks around your home.
- Call your doctor if your headaches get worse.

**Week 3:**
- You might feel able to do a few more light activities.
- Resume your normal daily activities as tolerated.
- Eat your regular diet.
- You should not have shortness of breath or chest pain.
- Watch for fevers over 100.5 degrees Fahrenheit.
- Your goal this week is to increase your walking time slightly.
- Call your doctor if you have new shortness of breath or chest pain.

**Week 4:**
- Your energy levels should continue to improve.
- You can gradually return to your usual activities.
- Keep eating your regular diet.
- Your headaches should be gone or very mild.
- Watch for fevers over 100.5 degrees Fahrenheit.
- Your goal this week is to walk for about 15 minutes each day.
- Call your doctor if you have a fever over 100.5.

**When to expect improvement:**
- You should feel better each week.
- Healing takes time and patience.
- Keep following up with your doctor.
- Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor.
escalation_guide:
CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY
These symptoms are life-threatening. Do not drive yourself.
- Trouble breathing: Your body needs oxygen now.
- Chest pain: Your heart needs help now.
- Uncontrolled bleeding: Bleeding needs to stop right away.
- Signs of stroke: Face droops. Arm feels weak. Trouble speaking.
- Sudden confusion: This can be a serious sign.
- Loss of consciousness: You passed out and will not wake.

GO TO THE ER TODAY
Do not wait until tomorrow. Go within a few hours.
- Fevers greater than 100.5: You may have an infection.
- Bleeding that will not stop: Bleeding needs urgent care.
- Bad headache with stiff neck: This can be serious.
- Vomiting blood or it looks like coffee grounds: This is an emergency.
- Black, tarry stools: This needs urgent care now.
- New or worsening leg swelling: This could be a blood clot.
- Trouble breathing or shortness of breath: This needs check now.

CALL YOUR DOCTOR
Call during office hours. Do not go to the ER for these.
- Questions about your medicine: Your nurse can help you plan.
- Feeling tired or weak: This can be part of your problem.
- Not wanting to eat: This can happen with your illness.
- Mild nausea: You feel a little sick to your stomach.
